definition: To finally give in or soften after refusing or resisting for a while.
example: After a week of pleading, my grandmother relented and let us paint the porch purple.
nuance: Relent implies softening after firm resistance, while yield can mean giving way at once to force or pressure.
prompt: Campers beg their counselor to let them stay up past lights-out.
options: The counselor held firm for an hour but chose to relent and allow twenty extra minutes.
The counselor asked a camper to relent his flashlight so she could check the trail.
The counselor chose to relent by banning flashlights and moving lights-out half an hour earlier.
The counselor seemed to relent the campers for keeping the whole cabin awake.
reasons: She resisted at first and then eased her stance, which is giving way after refusing.
Relent takes no object; handing an item over would be relinquishing or lending it.
Tightening the rules is the opposite of easing up after resistance.
Feeling bitter toward someone is resenting them, not softening a firm position.

practice.prompt: Students keep asking their teacher to postpone a quiz.
options: To relent, the teacher added a second quiz and made the first one twice as long.
The teacher had wanted to delay the quiz from the very start, so she was thrilled to relent.
When half the class caught the flu, the teacher decided to relent and move the quiz.
The student began to relent for copying a classmate's homework last week.
reasons: Piling on more work hardens a position instead of softening it.
Giving in requires earlier resistance; going along with your own plan is not yielding.
She had refused before but softened when circumstances changed, which is giving in.
Feeling sorry for a past wrong is repenting; this word means easing a stance.
